glossary.ld_sweep: The advisor flies one simulation per rail setting (inclination × heading) with the wind shown below and keeps the setting whose landing point is closest to the pad among those that pass every hard check.
glossary.ld_apogee_max: Competition rule: the highest point of the flight, measured from the ground at the pad, must not go above the limit.
glossary.ld_apogee_recommended: The guide recommends that simulations stay below this height, to keep a margin for what the simulation cannot know.
glossary.ld_tilt_max: How far the rail leans from vertical (90° minus the inclination). The rules do not allow a rail tilted more than the limit.
glossary.ld_static_margin_min: The stability margin is the distance from the centre of mass to the centre of pressure, in body diameters (calibres). It must stay above the limit during the whole ascent, otherwise the rocket can turn into the wind or tumble.
glossary.ld_descent_max: The speed at which the rocket reaches the ground under its parachute. Above the limit it breaks the rule and can damage the rocket.
glossary.ld_descent_recommended: The guide recommends landing within this speed range: slow enough to protect the rocket, fast enough not to drift far.
glossary.ld_landing_radius: How far from the pad the rocket lands. The guide recommends landing inside this radius so the team can find and recover it.
glossary.ld_rail_exit_min: The speed when the rocket leaves the rail. Below it the fins cannot yet keep the rocket pointing straight. This is common practice, not a rule of the guide.
glossary.ld_wind_max: The wind used in the simulation. Above the limit the rocket may not go to the rail.
glossary.apogee: The highest point the rocket reaches before it starts falling back down.
glossary.mach: Speed compared to the speed of sound. Mach 1 means the rocket is moving as fast as sound (~343 m/s at sea level).
glossary.rail_departure: The moment the rocket leaves the launch rail. A faster, more stable departure means a straighter, safer flight.
glossary.stability_margin: How stable the rocket is, measured in calibers (body diameters). Roughly 1–2 cal is a healthy, controllable flight.
glossary.forecast: Real weather forecast (GFS) for your launch date and place. Available for dates within about 16 days from now.
glossary.standard_atmosphere: A textbook average atmosphere. Used when no real forecast is available — good for a quick, repeatable estimate.
glossary.mc_counts: Attempted is how many flights were simulated. Succeeded are the ones that finished and are used in the results. Failed are the ones the simulator could not complete; they are left out.
glossary.mc_apogee_stats: Mean ± std is the average apogee and how much the flights typically differ from it (one standard deviation). P5, Median and P95 bracket the flights: 5 % were lower than P5, half were lower than the median and 5 % were higher than P95, so 90 % of the flights reached between P5 and P95.
glossary.mc_histogram: Each bar counts the flights whose apogee fell in that range of heights. A tall, narrow shape means the flights agree; a wide, flat one means the apogee is hard to predict.
glossary.mc_ellipses: Each ellipse is an area where the rocket lands: about 39 % of landings fall inside 1σ, 86 % inside 2σ and 99 % inside 3σ (the outer one). The marker is the launch site. The ellipses come from the simulated spread of the inputs, not from a real wind forecast unless the scenario used one.

montecarlo.readNone: No flight could be simulated, so there is nothing to read yet.
montecarlo.explainerWhat: A Monte Carlo run repeats the same simulation many times. Each time, the inputs you cannot know exactly (mass, thrust, wind, launch angle and heading, rail length, as listed above) change a little at random.
montecarlo.explainerWhy: That is why the result is a spread, not a single number: it shows the range a real flight is likely to fall in.
montecarlo.explainerAltitude: Use the apogee range to check your target altitude and to choose a launch window with suitable conditions.
montecarlo.explainerSafety: Use the outer ellipse to choose the launch site and size the safety area: almost every landing falls inside it.
montecarlo.explainerMeasure: If the spread is too wide, find the input that matters most and measure it better (for example, weigh the rocket or check the motor data).
